name: フルーツむらはた 本店 (Fruit Murahata Honten)

claims.text: Built around fresh seasonal fruit, so naturally fruit-forward, though parfaits include dairy and wheat-based items.
Soba shops typically blend buckwheat with wheat flour and share boiling water and fryers with wheat udon and tempura; no gluten-free handling is documented.
Broth/tsuyu is dashi- and soy-sauce-based, and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat.
Dashi broth is fish/bonito based and the menu features tempura, fish, and pork dishes; no vegan preparation is indicated.
As a traditional sushi restaurant, soy sauce (which normally contains wheat) is integral to the meal; no gluten-free or wheat-free soy sauce is documented.
The menu is centered on raw fish and seafood, so vegan diners would face pervasive fish/seafood contact with no documented plant-based options.

name: 源左ェ門 片町店 (Genzaemon Katamachi-ten)

claims.text: Core dishes such as jibuni and grilled fish are seasoned with soy sauce and dashi, which normally contain wheat; no gluten-free soy sauce is documented.

name: 御料理 五十嵐 (Goryori Igarashi)

claims.text: Traditional kaiseki built on dashi and soy-based seasonings; standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, and there is no documented gluten-free handling.
Kaga kaiseki cooking relies on soy sauce and dashi throughout the courses; assume wheat-containing soy sauce is used.
Courses are seafood- and dashi-centric with animal products in nearly every dish; no plant-only option is documented.

Core dishes are breaded and deep-fried (pork cutlets, fried swordfish, fried shrimp) in shared oil, and roux-based curry and tartar-sauced omelet rice all contain wheat, so cross-contamination is unavoidable.
Egg and meat are central to nearly every dish (omurice, Hanton Rice, cutlets, meat curry); a shared fryer and griddle make vegan-safe preparation impractical.
Kaga cuisine such as jibuni and the restaurant's simmered and braised dishes rely on Japanese soy sauce and dashi, which typically contain wheat; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
The kitchen is built around fish, shellfish, duck and fish-based dashi; cross-contact with animal products is effectively unavoidable and no plant-based menu is documented.
Traditional sushi counter where wheat-containing soy sauce is central to the meal; no gluten-free handling is documented, so cross-contact with gluten should be assumed.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (typically brewed with wheat) is used for nigiri and sashimi; no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.
Seafood-centric omakase; dishes are prepared on shared surfaces with fish, so no vegan-safe preparation is available.
